analysis.one_liner: Gave states federal grants and legal waivers to build their own universal health coverage systems, including single-payer plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on June 10, 2009, referred to four House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let up to ten states get federal planning grants and up to five states get demonstration grants to build universal health coverage for all their residents, with benefits at least as rich as a standard federal employee plan. It would have let states pool Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health money, get federal waivers (including a waiver of the ERISA law that normally blocks states from regulating employer health plans), and require that at least one approved state test a single-payer system. The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and never advanced; it died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, uninsured and underinsured residents of participating states would have gained guaranteed coverage regardless of income, employment, or preexisting conditions, with benefits at least equal to a standard federal employee plan. States that wanted to test single-payer or other simplified-administration systems would have gained federal start-up money, a 3-percentage-point boost to their federal Medicaid matching rate, and legal waivers — including relief from ERISA, the federal law that normally prevents states from restructuring employer-based insurance.

how_it_helps.text: It would have funded up to 10 states to plan, and up to 5 states to implement, systems covering every resident regardless of income, employment, or preexisting condition.

It would have let participating states pool federal health dollars — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee coverage — and, at a state's option, run a single-payer system with one payer and simplified administration.
It would have waived ERISA's preemption of state health regulation, the main legal barrier that stops states from reforming employer-based insurance.

It required that federal payments continue and that benefits not be reduced for people moving from federal programs into the state system, and protected residents who moved to a non-participating state by letting them re-enroll in federal programs immediately.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would have paid planning grants up to $4.5 million per state, transition grants up to $13 million plus $4 per resident per demonstration state, and a 3-percentage-point increase in each participating state's federal Medicaid match — while continuing to pay the federal health funds that would flow into the state's pool. Health insurers would have lost customers and revenue in any state that adopted a single-payer system, and employer plans there would have been folded into the state system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; insurers in demo states

drawbacks.text: The bill authorized substantial federal spending — up to $4.5 million per planning grant and up to $13 million plus $4 per resident in transition aid per demonstration state, with a 3-percentage-point boost to each state's federal Medicaid matching rate — costs a fiscal conservative would question before results were proven.

By waiving ERISA's preemption and allowing states to pool Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based funds, the bill would have let states displace existing private employer coverage, an outcome critics view as a step toward a government-run system and an upheaval for people satisfied with their current insurance.
Only 10 planning grants and 5 demonstration grants were available nationwide, so most states and their residents would have gotten nothing from the program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits were large for the states that would have participated: federal funding and legal waivers to build universal coverage without losing Medicare and Medicaid dollars, plus a guaranteed slot for a single-payer model to be tested in the real world. The costs were also real: the federal government would have taken on hundreds of millions in grants and foregone cost-sharing, and consolidation of all payers into one state system would have carried transition risks for hospitals, insurers, and patients alike. The main design criticism is that the bill put public money behind experiments that could, in states choosing single-payer, eliminate the private insurance market there — precisely the feature supporters saw as the point and opponents saw as the threat.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee without ever being taken up, dying quietly when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: After introduction on June 10, 2009, the bill was referred to four committees and, a day later, to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and its last recorded action is the subcommittee referral.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and other health interests that a state-run universal system could have displaced were spared any test of that model; states and their uninsured residents got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers whose markets stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich and Rep. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Democrats were involved and no votes occurred, so no partisan shape can be read from the record.

industries.note: In states that chose a single-payer model, private insurers would have lost their role as payers for most residents' coverage. The bill's demonstration design and benefit floor made that outcome a real possibility, which is why it threatened the industry's core market.

Providers would have gained universal coverage for their patients and simpler administration, but would have faced a single payer with strong power to hold down payments in states that consolidated financing.
